The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02225
Nor can we accept the impression that the movement began simply because Wāṣil moved from one study circle in the mosque of Basra to another circle in the same mosque.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02226

Taken literally, that story makes Muʿtazilism appear to have arisen suddenly and spontaneously from a brief physical act: one man, moved by the emotion of the moment, changing his seat by a few steps.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02227
To understand a historical and intellectual movement of this kind in such a way would be more than a crude oversimplification. It would seriously distort the nature of historical change itself.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02228
There is no reason to think that al-Shahrastānī or the other historians who preserved this story intended such an oversimplification or distortion.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02229
They gave us the historical material available to them. It is we, reading that material, who interpret it according to the methods each of us uses in research and historical analysis.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02230

There are, in any case, other historical accounts of the origins of the Muʿtazila that make it much clearer that the name referred to an intellectual position shared by a broader current, not simply to an individual person or to his physical movement from one place to another.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02231
Al-Isfarāyīnī, for example, says that the Muʿtazila received their name because “they withdrew from the circle of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and withdrew from the position of the Muslims.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02232
The important point here is that both “Muʿtazila” and “Muslims” appear in the plural.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02233

This points us toward the idea itself: Muʿtazilism was a broader intellectual movement. The Muʿtazila as a group thought differently from the Muslim majority as a group on certain questions of belief.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02234
Ṭāshkubrīzāda gives another account that suggests that the name “Muʿtazila” did not originally come from the Muʿtazilites themselves, but from some of their opponents.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02235

He reports that Qatāda ibn Diʿāma al-Sadūsī, who died in 117 or 118 AH, was blind but used to move around Basra without a guide. One day he entered the mosque of Basra and came upon ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd sitting with a group of men. Thinking that this was al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī’s circle, he approached them. When he realized that it was not, he said:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02236
“These are only the Muʿtazila.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02237
He then got up and left them.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02238
According to the account, they were called the Muʿtazila from that day onward.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02239
We also have a statement from one of the leading Muʿtazilite thinkers, Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02240
“Every use of the word ‘withdrawal’ in the Qurʾān means withdrawing from falsehood. We therefore know that the name Muʿtazila is a term of praise.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02241
This is more a defense than a neutral historical statement.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02242

It suggests that the name “Muʿtazila” had become widely used as a term of criticism or condemnation. Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār was trying to answer the insult intended by the Muʿtazila’s opponents and turn the name instead into something praiseworthy.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02243
5 — Toward a New Intellectual Method
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02244
From everything we have seen so far, it becomes clear that the Muʿtazila were not mistaken when they regarded al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī as the head of their school, as Ibn Khallikān reports.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02245

They did so even though historians claim that their very name, “Muʿtazila,” came from the incident in which Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ “withdrew” from the circle of his teacher, al-Ḥasan, after they disagreed over the status of a person who commits a major sin.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02246
That incident may appear to mark a clear dividing line between al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and the Muʿtazila, or even a historical moment when al-Ḥasan’s school and theirs separated.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02247

But to define the relationship between al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Muʿtazilism on the basis of this incident alone is to begin from an idealist and subjective viewpoint, far removed from a proper analysis of historical movements.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02248
We have already seen that explaining the name “Muʿtazila” simply through this one individual incident also removes the movement from its real historical setting.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02249
The Muʿtazila themselves took a broader view when they called al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī the “head of the school.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02250

We do not need to take the word “head” literally. What matters is the deeper point behind it: there was a strong and positive connection between al-Ḥasan’s school and the school that later became the Muʿtazila.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02251
And this connection went further than the fact that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī accepted the Qadarite belief in freedom, or that his school became an early center for teaching and spreading that belief.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02252
Neither of those facts is unimportant. But the relationship runs deeper than both.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02253
What matters most is the kind of intellectual method al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī used—apparently for the first time in the development of Arab-Islamic thought.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02254
It does not matter here what first led him to use this method, whether he understood clearly what he was doing, understood it only in a general way, or arrived at it spontaneously.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02255
What was this method?
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02256

To understand it, we first need to look at how the political parties of the time, and the intellectual movements that spoke for them, had previously dealt with questions such as the status of someone who commits a major sin or the problem of divine decree and human freedom.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02257
As we have already seen, these questions were originally discussed in a direct and practical way. People approached them through the real events that had made the questions urgent in the first place.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02258
To put this more plainly, when people debated the status of someone who had committed a major sin, they wanted their conclusions to apply directly to particular people.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02259
They were thinking about the killers of ʿUthmān, about Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr, about ʿĀʾisha, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Muʿāwiya, the Umayyad caliphs in general, or even the Umayyad state as a whole.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02260
The same was true of the debate over divine decree.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02261
We saw how Maʿbad al-Juhanī and ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār came to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and said:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02262
“Abū Saʿīd, these rulers consider it lawful to shed Muslim blood and seize Muslim wealth, and then they say: ‘Our actions simply happen according to God’s decree.’”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02263
Maʿbad and ʿAṭāʾ were approaching the question in its immediate, concrete setting. They were thinking about these rulers and their actions.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02264
But when al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī entered the discussion, something changed.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02265
For whatever objective reason, he shifted the debate—especially the question of the person who commits a major sin—away from particular cases and into a more abstract form.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02266
He moved from the specific to the general, from people to concepts, from individual cases to broader categories.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02267
His method was therefore becoming more theoretical.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02268

Instead of dealing first with particular people, he took “the person who commits a major sin” as a subject in its own right. He treated it as a general question, or concept, apart from the specific people involved in the controversy at that moment.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02269
He then examined the issue on that level and concluded that a person who commits a major sin is a hypocrite, not an unbeliever.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02270
This means that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī took the first step toward the method that the Muʿtazila would later use in their theoretical investigations.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02271

The relationship between al-Ḥasan’s school and the Muʿtazilite tradition of rational inquiry therefore went much deeper than their shared belief in freedom of choice, or the role his teaching circle played in spreading that belief.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02272

The method whose first step we see in al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī—and we do not deny Jahm ibn Ṣafwān’s own contribution to abstract reasoning—helped Arab-Islamic thought begin moving toward a degree of independence of its own.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02273

We gradually begin to see the signs of this among the Muʿtazila. Their work helped prepare the ground for kalām to become a developed intellectual discipline in its own right, and kalām, in turn, helped prepare the way for the emergence of philosophy.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02274
At first, this may seem to contradict what we argued earlier.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02275

We spent considerable effort showing that these intellectual questions were rooted in political and social conditions. Yet we are now speaking about thought becoming relatively independent in dealing with those same questions.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02276
But there is no basic contradiction between thought being connected to objective reality—to material conditions—and thought gaining a degree of independence of its own.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02277

When we say that questions arising in Arab-Islamic society at a particular historical moment were reflected in the minds of thinkers in a particular way, we mean that human thought does not create the raw material of its ideas out of itself.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02278
The mind does not produce that material entirely from within, cut off from the world around it.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02279
Take the problem of divine decree.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02280
Arab-Islamic thought did not suddenly become interested in this question for no reason.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02281

Political, social, and religious conditions had forced people in that particular society to decide where they stood toward certain social groups, toward particular individuals who represented one group or another, and toward religious texts that shaped their behavior and beliefs.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02282
People also had to interpret those texts in ways that reflected their political and class positions.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02283
Because people differed in those positions, thinkers differed as well.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02284
But another question then arises: How does thought express its position? How does it represent the people, events, and situations outside itself?
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02285
At an earlier stage in its historical development, thought remains closely tied to the immediate forms in which the outside world appears.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02286
It works within the concrete situations directly presented by reality and remains bound to its experience of those situations.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02287

At a more advanced stage, however, thought becomes able to take what it receives from the outside world, break it down, and put it together again without remaining tied to each particular form in which it first appeared.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02288
This process of analysis and combination is abstraction itself.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02289
Thought takes many individual, material experiences, sets aside the features unique to each one, and draws from them a broader and more general concept.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02290
This is what we mean by the relative independence of abstract thought.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02291

Thought can become more independent, but only up to a point. The mind can analyze, combine, and generalize what it experiences, but it does not create its raw material from nothing. That still comes from the world around us.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02292
And thought can achieve this kind of relative independence only after reaching a fairly advanced stage in its historical development.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02293
The contradiction therefore disappears.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02294

There is no conflict between our earlier argument—that previous intellectual movements were connected to the political and social struggles of early Islam—and what we have now tried to show in the case of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: that his method helped prepare the way for a new current of rational inquiry into Islamic belief, later represented to a large extent by the Muʿtazila.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02295
We will try to show this more clearly through examples from the way the Muʿtazila themselves explained the principles of their school.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02296
One further point remains about the intellectual development we have identified in al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī’s method.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02297
It might be argued that al-Ḥasan simply acted out of the same weakness toward Umayyad intimidation that we have discussed before.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02298

In other words, perhaps he moved the question of the person who commits a major sin away from concrete cases and into the abstract—from the particular to the general, from people to concepts—because he wanted to avoid confronting the practical political issue.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02299
Perhaps, to protect himself from the anger of the rulers, he preferred to move the debate onto the safer ground of pure theory.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02300
In our view, this is quite possible.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02301
There is a strong chance that this was indeed part of al-Ḥasan’s motive.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02302
But our concern here is not with the intention behind his action, or with the psychological reason that led him to it.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02303
Our concern is with the action itself.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02304
Whatever his motive, the way al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī approached the question shows that this major thinker genuinely helped prepare the way for the rational method later developed by the Muʿtazila.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02305
The Basic Principles of Muʿtazilite Doctrine
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02306
Historians of the Islamic sects divide the Muʿtazila into a number of different groups or schools. Each is usually named after one of its leading thinkers.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02307
Thus we find, for example, the Wāṣiliyya, named after Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, and the Naẓẓāmiyya, named after Ibrāhīm ibn Sayyār al-Naẓẓām, and so on.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02308
Al-Malaṭī counted twenty Muʿtazilite groups. Al-Baghdādī raised the number to twenty-two. Al-Shahrastānī lists twelve.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02309
Historians also divide them geographically into the Muʿtazila of Basra and the Muʿtazila of Baghdad.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02310
One account says:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02311

“Muʿtazilism first appeared in Basra because Abū Ḥudhayfa Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ brought it there from Medina. It is said that the Muʿtazila of Baghdad took Muʿtazilism from the Muʿtazila of Basra. The first of the Baghdad Muʿtazila was Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir. He traveled to Basra and met Bishr ibn Saʿīd and Abū ʿUthmān al-Zaʿfarānī, both companions of Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, and learned Muʿtazilism from them. He then carried Muʿtazilism and the Five Principles to Baghdad.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02312
These Five Principles were:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02313
Divine Unity, Justice, the Promise and the Threat, the Position Between the Two Positions, and Commanding What Is Right and Forbidding What Is Wrong.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02314
However many different groups the Muʿtazila divided into, these Five Principles were what united them.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02315
The differences between the various Muʿtazilite schools concerned what they called the secondary questions that followed from these principles.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02316

Those differences grew as the school itself developed. They became more pronounced as its leading thinkers came into greater contact with philosophy from different outside sources, and as Arab-Islamic thought became more closely connected with philosophical traditions—especially Greek philosophy after translation spread widely under the Abbasids.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02317
Historians of the Islamic sects do not disagree about which basic principles united the different Muʿtazilite groups, although they sometimes present them differently.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02318

Al-Shahrastānī, for example, gives four principles rather than five. This is because he combines two of them into one, treating “the Position Between the Two Positions” as part of “the Promise and the Threat.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02319
The Muʿtazila themselves also recognized these Five Principles as what united their school.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02320
Al-Khayyāṭ, for example, the author of The Book of Triumph and one of the leading Muʿtazilite thinkers of the third Islamic century, or ninth century CE, writes:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02321

“No one deserves to be called a Muʿtazilite until he accepts all Five Principles: Divine Unity, Justice, the Promise and the Threat, the Position Between the Two Positions, and Commanding What Is Right and Forbidding What Is Wrong. When all these principles are present in a person, he is a Muʿtazilite.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02322
Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, who led a Muʿtazilite school named after him and died in 235 AH, early in the caliphate of the Abbasid ruler al-Mutawakkil, is also said to have:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02323

“written a book for the Muʿtazila in which he explained their school and gathered together their teachings. He called the book The Five Principles. Whenever they met a man, they would quietly ask him: ‘Have you read The Five Principles?’ If he said yes, they knew that he followed their school.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02324
Al-Shahrastānī begins his discussion of the Muʿtazila by saying:
